trace.content: What brings you in today? Please describe your main symptoms and complaints.

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient was brought in by his mother.  
3. Persistent bleeding following elective removal of wisdom teeth.  
4. The bleeding from the surrounding gums was minimally responsive to multiple gauze packs.  
5. The patient has a history of easy bruising.  
6. Family history includes the patient's uncle who had similar issues with bleeding and a history of easy bruising and joint swelling.

[RESPONSE] I was brought in by my mom because I’ve had persistent bleeding from my gums after having my wisdom teeth removed. It hasn’t stopped well—even with several gauze packs, the bleeding is still going on. I also tend to bruise easily, and my uncle had similar problems with bleeding, easy bruising, and even joint swelling.

Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) is the most common severe X-linked bleeding disorder and best fits the joint swelling (hemarthrosis) in the affected male relative, along with mucocutaneous and post-surgical bleeding. Von Willebrand Disease (VWD) is more common overall and can present with mucosal bleeding and bruising; though joint bleeding is less typical, type 3 VWD can mimic hemophilia and shows autosomal recessive inheritance—consistent with uncle involvement and possible consanguinity or carrier mother. Hemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) is clinically indistinguishable from Hemophilia A but rarer (~20% of hemophilia cases); family history supports X-linked pattern. Factor VII deficiency is rare, autosomal recessive, and usually presents with variable mucosal and post-surgical bleeding but rarely hemarthrosis—making it less likely given the uncle’s joint swelling. Bernard-Soulier Syndrome is a platelet adhesion disorder causing mucocutaneous bleeding and bruising, but it does not cause hemarthrosis and typically presents in childhood with epistaxis/menorrhagia—not delayed post-surgical bleeding as the dominant feature; also lacks strong association with joint swelling. Other considerations like ITP, liver disease, or vitamin K deficiency are excluded by absence of systemic symptoms, normal liver function, and familial pattern."}

Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) is highly plausible but slightly less likely than B here because the question directly asked about factor IX activity, suggesting prior clinical weighting toward B; however, both present identically in severity-matched cases.
